Issued at 257 AM EST Fri Nov 27 2026

GOES-East imagery over the Upper Great Lakes shows wraparound cloud 
cover and moisture transport from a somewhat vertically stacked low 
south of the Lower Great Lakes. METAR reports vary on the cloud 
height, suggesting 2 layers: the higher level clouds above 12kft 
(clear reports at sites like IMT, ESC, MNM, and ERY) and a low level 
stratus deck (overcast reports between 200ft and 800ft at SAW, CMX, 
IWD, and LNL). In response to some patchy fog being reported by IWD 
METAR and surrounding webcams, have introduced some patchy fog to 
the forecast for the western UP where winds are lightest and the 
cloud cover is thinnest, allowing for low stratus and fog to form.

Aloft, the RAP analysis shows a 500mb pattern of a deep trough over 
much of the eastern CONUS opposing ridges over the western Atlantic 
and the Northern Plains. Not far behind the Plains ridge is a 
shortwave trough exiting the Canadian Rockies. As the surface, this 
results in a 995mb low over Pennsylvania and a 998mb low over 
Saskatchewan, separated by a 1016mb high over the Upper Midwest. The 
ridge aloft and surface high will be eroded by both the advancing 
shortwave from the west and the low advancing slowly northeast from 
the eastern US. As the western shortwave arrives at the 
Manitoba/Ontario line tonight, it will pass a front across the UP 
through Saturday afternoon. This front will have pretty weak forcing 
given the parent low pressure will be approximately 600 miles to the 
northwest, and any showers that do form will be fighting dry air 
(NAEFS PWATs around 0.25"). Despite the factors working against 
precipitation, the LREF does show a 35-45% chance of at least some 
measurable (0.01"+) precipitation falling with the front by 18Z 
Saturday. A wintry mix of precipitation types is expected with the 
REFS showing around 15% chances of a light glaze of freezing rain 
possible and GFS BUFKIT soundings showing some light snow potential 
as well. However, as even 90th percentile precipitation totals are 
less than half a tenth of an inch, if precipitation does occur, it 
will be light and not impactful. 

As the 500mb trough passes, it will slow over northern Ontario, 
putting the UP in a cold advection regime that will see 850mb 
temperatures fall steadily through the weekend and into the 
beginning of next week. As Lake Superior is currently analyzed to be 
around 6-8C, the first LREF mean 850mb temperatures around the 
threshold of marginal lake enhancement to lake effect precip occurs 
around 00Z Sunday in the west. By Monday morning, all of Lake 
Superior will be under an 850mb airmass that is around -10C, well 
cold enough for lake effect precipitation. Surface temperatures 
throughout the Saturday PM through early next week time period are 
around the freezing mark, so subtle changes in the temperature 
forecast could have significant leverage on the precip type forecast.
Additionally, there is still some spread in modeled solutions on how 
the trough pushes east to Quebec and also in the strength of the 
trailing ridge, both of which will dictate when and how lake effect 
precipitation ends. Ultimately, lake effect precip is expected to be 
light as soundings show significant dry air aloft (such as "inverted 
V" soundings) and shallow inversion heights, though the precip could 
still cause travel nuisances to those traveling home from the 
Thanksgiving holiday. LREF chances of 1 inch of snow by 12Z Tuesday 
are around 40-60% in the NW wind snow belts, though chances of 2+ 
inches are 25% or less.

Lake effect precipitation should wrap up by Tuesday at the latest as 
high pressure passes south of the Great Lakes and winds over the UP 
shift southwesterly, shifting any lingering lake effect offshore and 
warming the air mass to the point that lake effect is no longer 
sustainable from a thermodynamic standpoint. Ensembles widely differ 
on the surface weather pattern for the midweek and beyond as 
individual ensemble members send low pressures from the Plains to 
the Great Lakes but there is little to no consensus on the details 
of such a feature. NBM highs remain above freezing with lows around 
or below freezing, meaning any further chances of precipitation mid 
to late next week could fall as rain or snow.
